out.other_title: AI safety via debate: zero-sum self-play debate game judged by a human
out.rationale: The authors take Irving et al.'s debate tree directly and change how it is used: the full-tree expansion becomes an explicit reference computation M whose outputs the authors' debate protocol aims to produce more efficiently. M calls (simulated) human judges to adjudicate every individual path through the tree, whereas in Irving et al.'s game a human judges a single debate, and the authors only hypothesize that M would produce correct outputs within the question domain. No record states the debate-tree analogy, so the paper-level record is used. The citing passage names the cited work; the target is the cited paper's main record, not a record of the specific result.
out.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Using the full debate tree from Irving et al. as the reference computation M, which the authors hypothesize would produce correct outputs within the question domain and whose outputs their debate protocol aims to produce more efficiently; holds for the authors' safety-case argument structure

text: The authors reproduce Irving et al.'s figure (Figure 8) as an analogy between debate and Go: in both cases a single game with strong players is evidence as to which moves were best. They say their M is equivalent to expanding the whole tree, a computation that produces every possible argument and counterargument at every stage and calls (simulated) human judges to adjudicate every path through the tree; they hypothesize it would produce correct outputs within the question domain, and the goal of their debate protocol is to produce the same outputs more efficiently.
title: Buhl et al. reproduce Irving et al.'s debate-Go analogy; their M expands the whole tree
